facts.text: It has a pale buff-orange throat blending into a soft, creamy-yellow breast, with black legs and bill.
facts.quote: Their throat and chin is a pale buff-orange that blends into the soft, creamy-yellow of the breast. Legs, toes, and bill are all black.

facts.text: It makes a loud two-note tzid-id call, harsher and less insect-like than that of the striated thornbill.
facts.quote: The yellow thornbill has a loud, two-note tzid-id call, notably different from calls of the closely related striated thornbill by its harsher, less insect-like sound.

facts.text: The call is used to keep in touch while foraging, for defence, and to advertise territory.
facts.quote: The call is repeated at various intervals throughout the day and is associated with contact between birds while foraging, as defence, or as a territorial advertisement.

facts.text: Its rounded, domed nest has a small entrance near the top and is held together with spider-web.
facts.quote: Yellow thornbill nests are rounded and domed, with a small entrance near the top. Nests are usually made of bark-fibre and grasses matted together with spider-web, located in the upper foliage of shrubs and small trees.

facts.text: It mainly eats insects, sometimes snatching them mid-flight, and will occasionally eat seeds.
facts.quote: Their diet consists mostly of insects, but they will sometimes eat seeds. They will also catch insects mid-flight.

facts.text: It forages in the upper and middle canopy, moving rapidly through outer foliage and even looking under bark.
facts.quote: They prefer the upper and middle levels of forest canopy, and can be found moving rapidly through the outer foliage searching for food, or looking under bark.

facts.text: It prefers vegetation dominated by casuarinas or eucalypts, especially in drier climates.
facts.quote: yellow thornbills are found in a variety of habitats including shrublands, forests and thickets, preferring vegetation dominated by casuarinas or eucalypts, particularly in areas with a drier climate.

facts.text: Juveniles look like adults but with softer, duller feathers and a still-yellow gape when recently fledged.
facts.quote: Juveniles appear similar to adults, though feathers are "softer" looking and duller by comparison . When recently fledged, their gape is still yellow.

facts.text: Clutches of two to four eggs are incubated for 16–17 days soon after the nest is completed.
facts.quote: Clutches of two to four eggs are laid soon after the nest has been completed, and are incubated for 16–17 days.

facts.text: It usually breeds in solitary pairs, though cooperative breeding has been found in some areas.
facts.quote: The yellow thornbill likely breed in solitary pairs, but in some areas, evidence of co-operative breeding has been found.
